title: Sacral and Implantable Tibial Neuromodulation for the Management of Overactive Bladder: A Systematic Review and Meta‑analysis
article_subtype: Systematic review with an indirect comparison using single-arm study results
condition_or_topic: Overactive bladder (OAB), including urgency urinary incontinence (UUI), and its treatment with implantable neuromodulation.
clinical_background: OAB can involve urgency, frequent urination, nocturia, and UUI, and can substantially affect quality of life. Approximately one in six adults in the United States and Europe has OAB. Sacral neuromodulation (SNM) is an established implantable treatment, while implantable tibial neuromodulation (iTNM) has recently become commercially available in the US as a less invasive option. Direct comparative studies of the two approaches were unavailable.
objectives: Indirectly compare the efficacy and safety of SNM and iTNM for OAB by synthesizing results from studies of each treatment.
Assess similarities and differences in symptom response and adverse events, including responses in UUI, urinary frequency, and overall OAB symptoms.
clinical_question: In adults with OAB and/or UUI (Patient), how does iTNM (Intervention) compare indirectly with SNM (Comparator) for symptom improvement and device- or procedure-related adverse events (Outcome)?
interpretation: The indirect analysis found broadly similar efficacy and safety for iTNM and SNM in treating OAB and UUI, including symptom response, fewer UUI episodes and improved quality of life. iTNM showed this comparable efficacy despite the absence of a pre-implantation stimulation trial, whereas most SNM studies used such a trial to exclude nonresponders. Patient-reported improvement and satisfaction tended to favor iTNM. Lower surgical re-intervention rates with iTNM remain a possibility rather than an established long-term difference because follow-up was shorter. Both approaches had low rates of device- and procedure-related adverse events.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors place these findings alongside the established efficacy and safety of SNM and the prior evidence supporting tibial nerve stimulation. They note that the favorable efficacy results from the ARTISAN SNM study were obtained without a stimulation trial, while most other included SNM studies required one. They also cite an earlier patient-preference survey suggesting that iTNM may increase interest in minimally invasive OAB treatment. No previous head-to-head study of iTNM and SNM was identified.
clinical_implications: iTNM may offer patients with OAB another implantable treatment option with benefits similar to those observed for SNM, despite differences in stimulation site, implantation and treatment schedule.

The generally less invasive iTNM procedure and its favorable safety findings may broaden the options available to patients; individual preferences remain important because both procedures had favorable safety results.
Implantable neuromodulation offers a nonpharmacologic alternative in the context of concerns about a potential association between long-term anticholinergic use and dementia.
The lower observed rates of explantation and revision in iTNM studies cannot yet establish a durable advantage over SNM.
practice_implications: Treatment selection should account for patient and clinician preferences concerning the implantation procedure and the way patients interact with a device.

The differing demands of device use may matter to patients: the authors describe Revi as recommended for use at least once a day for 30 min, whereas other patients may prefer implanted systems requiring less frequent interaction.
The authors relate the availability of implantable neuromodulation to updated AUA/SUFU guidance supporting earlier consideration of minimally invasive OAB treatments.
limitations: No head-to-head trials were identified, preventing a direct comparison of efficacy and safety.

11 studies had a moderate risk of potential bias. The authors particularly identify difficulties with randomization and blinding when patients perceive stimulation, as well as retrospective and single-center study designs.
Differences in study populations, geographic settings, methods, definitions of efficacy and stages of device development may limit generalizability.
Patient-level data were unavailable, and not every study supplied data for every endpoint.
Weighted average follow-up was 13.0 months in iTNM studies versus 39.2 months in SNM studies, limiting comparisons of later revisions and explantations.
Published cost comparisons between iTNM and SNM were unavailable.

Marked regional differences in baseline urinary frequency complicated comparisons of that outcome: studies from North America, Europe and the Middle East reported a range of 10–14.9, versus 21.6–29.2 in SNM studies from Asia.
strengths: The meta-analysis included a large number of studies and patients.
The authors report that the similarity of key results across different study designs increased their confidence that the overall findings were representative.
open_questions: Whether comparable iTNM efficacy will persist with longer follow-up despite the absence of a pre-implantation trial remains uncertain.
Whether the lower observed iTNM revision and explantation rates will persist over longer follow-up remains uncertain.
The reason for the regional differences in baseline urinary frequency is unclear.
The comparative effect of iTNM on urinary frequency requires clarification.
The effect of differing requirements for patient interaction with devices on treatment selection is not yet well understood.
future_directions: Conduct randomized head-to-head studies to clarify comparative efficacy and safety and inform patient selection for tibial versus sacral neuromodulation.
Obtain longer-term iTNM data to assess whether efficacy remains comparable without a pre-implantation trial and to compare later revisions and explantations.
Investigate the effect of iTNM on urinary frequency.
Examine how requirements for device interaction affect patient selection as more clinical evidence becomes available.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of an indirect comparison between implantable tibial neuromodulation (iTNM) and sacral neuromodulation (SNM) for overactive bladder (OAB) and/or urgency urinary incontinence (UUI). The review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidance and was prospectively registered as PROSPERO ID CRD42024549598. Searches of PubMed and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) were conducted in May 2024 and supplemented by nonsystematic Google Scholar searches. Included designs comprised 3 RCTs, ten prospective interventional studies, one prospective observational study and six retrospective chart reviews. No direct comparative or placebo-controlled studies of iTNM and SNM were identified, so the meta-analysis used results from separate study arms.

population.description: Adults with OAB and/or UUI who received permanent iTNM or SNM implants. The analysis included 350 patients treated with iTNM in 4 studies and 1416 treated with SNM in 16 studies. Weighted mean age was 61.2 years old for iTNM (n = 350) and 57.0 years old for SNM (n = 1416). Prior or current OAB treatment did not itself restrict eligibility.
inclusion_criteria: Permanent implantation of SNM or iTNM for OAB and/or UUI.
A prospective or retrospective clinical study or randomized trial with ≥ 15 patients.
An adult study population and publication after January 1, 2010.
exclusion_criteria: Non-human studies; reviews, study protocols or health economics studies; and articles unavailable in English.
Studies enrolling only patients with previous SNM/iTNM failure or only patients continuing use of previously implanted devices.
Populations outside OAB and/or UUI, or concurrent use of multiple minimally invasive therapies.
Studies reporting none of the meta-analysis’s primary efficacy or safety endpoints.
To avoid overlapping populations reported at multiple timepoints, all but the publication with the longest follow-up were excluded.
Under the prespecified rule, studies at high risk of bias were excluded from further data extraction if they represented less than 15% of selected study citations.
population.mean_age: Weighted mean: 61.2 years old for iTNM (n = 350); 57.0 years old for SNM (n = 1416).

comparators: iTNM and SNM were compared indirectly using results from separate study arms; there were no head-to-head or placebo-controlled studies.

primary: Percentage of patients with ≥ 50% improvement in UUI symptoms, assessed from voiding diaries when available.
Percentage of patients with ≥ 50% improvement in OAB symptoms, using study-specific composites of voiding-diary changes when available.
Percentage of patients with ≥ 50% improvement in urinary frequency (UF) symptoms, when available.

Rates of device- or procedure-related adverse events, including reported infection, pain, lead migration and wound-healing events; surgical revision or removal rates and reasons for reintervention were also collected.
secondary: Mean decrease in UUI episodes and mean change in urinary frequency.
Short-term (< 6 month) effects on UUI episodes.
Patient-reported quality-of-life measures, including Overactive Bladder Questionnaire (OAB-q), and patient satisfaction.

statistical_methods: Available primary efficacy and safety results were summarized as weighted averages for each neuromodulation type. Key primary endpoints were also examined separately for interventional studies (RCTs and prospective interventional studies) and observational studies (prospective observational studies and retrospective reviews). Descriptive statistics and weighted averages were calculated in Microsoft Excel; graphical figures were produced with GraphPad Prism and Microsoft Excel. Two reviewers independently selected studies and extracted published aggregate data, resolving discrepancies by discussion or third-reviewer arbitration. Missing data were not imputed, patient-level data were unavailable, and the longest reported follow-up was used when a publication presented multiple timepoints.
follow_up: For iTNM studies, follow-up ranged from 12 months to 3 years, with a weighted mean of 13.0 months. For SNM studies, final follow-up ranged from 6 months to 9.7 years, with a weighted mean of 39.2 months.

safety_results.overall_adverse_events: Weighted device-related AE rates were 9.6% (n = 284) in iTNM studies and 12.7% (n = 434) in SNM studies. Weighted procedure-related AE rates were 10.6% (n = 151) for iTNM and 11.6% (n = 129) for SNM.
notable_adverse_events: Weighted device-related SAE rates were 0.3% (n = 350) for iTNM and 3.3% (n = 892) for SNM.

Weighted infection rates were 5.1% (n = 330) for iTNM and 3.7% (n = 437) for SNM; weighted pain rates were 4.7% (n = 330) and 8.5% (n = 1107), respectively; weighted wound-healing AE rates were 5.3% (n = 284) and 3.8% (n = 104), respectively.
Among iTNM devices with published data, device-related AE rates were 4.0% for Revi and 16.0% for eCoin; these rates belong to the respective devices.

Across studies reporting each measure, weighted permanent explant, surgical revision, and lead migration rates were 13.7% (n = 1143), 26.8% (n = 1011), and 5.6% (n = 589) for SNM, versus 1.0% (n = 171), 0.0% (n = 20), and 1.7% (n = 179) for iTNM, respectively. Follow-up was shorter for iTNM.
Reported reasons for surgical revision included battery depletion requiring exchange, lead migration, electrode failure, loss of effectiveness, and adverse events such as infection.

subgroup_analyses: By study design, the weighted UUI response rate was 71.3% (n = 350) in interventional iTNM studies, 74.0% (n = 661) in interventional SNM studies, and 66.5% (n = 289) in observational SNM studies. All four included iTNM studies were interventional.

By study design, the weighted OAB response rate was 79.4% (n = 171) for interventional iTNM, 82.5% (n = 393) for interventional SNM, and 64.7% (n = 367) for observational SNM. The authors described the results across designs as broadly similar and attributed much of the interventional-versus-observational SNM difference to the results of two Axonics studies [58, 59].

Of the 16 included SNM studies, 14 used a PNE or staged trial before permanent implantation and 2 Axonics studies [58, 59] did not. Among studies using a trial, the weighted trial failure rate was 27%; those patients were not permanently implanted or included in the subsequent SNM results. The iTNM studies did not use a pre-implantation trial.
secondary_results: The analysis included 20 studies and 1766 patients: 4 iTNM studies with 350 patients and 16 SNM studies with 1416 patients. Study designs comprised three RCTs, ten prospective interventional studies, one prospective observational study, and six retrospective chart reviews. The authors reported nine included studies with low potential bias and eleven with moderate potential bias; one additional high-bias study was excluded.

Mean UUI episodes per day at baseline had weighted averages of 4.6 (n = 350) for iTNM and 5.0 (n = 1150) for SNM. The corresponding weighted average decreases were 3.0 (n = 350; range 2.5–3.5) and 3.5 (n = 1150; range 1.6–7.1) UUI episodes, respectively; baseline ranges were 4.3–6.5 and 2.4–8.9.

Baseline urinary frequency had weighted averages of 10.2 voiding episodes per day (n = 171; range 10–12.4) for iTNM and 15.1 (n = 1041; range 11.6–29.2) for SNM. Weighted average decreases were 2.0 (n = 304; range 1.8–2.7) for iTNM and 5.5 (n = 1041; range 2.1–13.9) for SNM. The authors considered the difference in decreases likely related to differing baseline frequency; SNM studies completed in Asia reported baseline frequencies of 21.6–29.2 voiding episodes per day.

At 3 months, weighted UUI response rates (≥ 50%) were 69.0% (n = 197; range 68–69.3%) for iTNM and 76.8% (n = 631; range 53–87%) for SNM. At 6 months, they were 74.4% (n = 304; range 69–85%) and 67.9% (n = 721; range 53–94%), respectively.

For an OAB-q HRQoL improvement of ≥ 10 points, weighted proportions were 83.2% (n = 171; range 73–85%) with iTNM and 48.4% (n = 340; range 40–82%) with SNM. The SNM proportion came from only two studies. Weighted average HRQoL score improvements were 34.5 points (n = 133) with iTNM and 35.1 points (n = 427; range 29–39.2) with SNM.

Weighted proportions reporting PGI-I improvement were 88.5% (n = 197; range 70–94.2%) for iTNM and 74.9% (n = 207; range 68–89%) for SNM. Weighted therapy-satisfaction proportions were 95.0% (n = 151) and 75.5% (n = 334; range 53.6–94%), respectively.

Follow-up differed between treatment groups: iTNM studies had a weighted average of 13.0 months, with study follow-up ranging from 12 months to 3 years; SNM studies had a weighted average of 39.2 months, with final follow-up ranging from 6 months to 9.7 years. The authors cautioned that later revision and explant rates require further assessment.

Across studies, weighted average age was 61.2 years (n = 350) for iTNM and 57.0 years (n = 1416) for SNM; weighted female proportions were 98.0% (n = 350) and 87.5% (n = 1416), respectively. Weighted proportions with UUI were 98.9% (n = 350) and 83.3% (n = 1107), while weighted proportions previously treated with oral medications were 92.6% (n = 330) and 99.7% (n = 1175), respectively.

main_conclusion: Across 20 studies involving 1766 patients, the authors found similar improvements in OAB and UUI outcomes and low device- and procedure-related adverse-event rates with iTNM and SNM. Comparable efficacy occurred although the iTNM studies did not use a preimplantation trial; longer follow-up is needed to determine whether the apparently lower iTNM surgical re-intervention rates persist.
narrative_summary:
This systematic review and meta-analysis indirectly compared implantable tibial neuromodulation (iTNM) with sacral neuromodulation (SNM) for overactive bladder (OAB) and urgency urinary incontinence (UUI). It included 20 studies and 1766 permanently implanted patients: 350 received iTNM and 1416 received SNM. Because no head-to-head or placebo-controlled comparison of the two approaches was identified, the authors used weighted averages from single-arm results.

A ≥ 50% improvement in UUI was reported for 71.3% of iTNM recipients (n = 350) and 71.8% of SNM recipients (n = 950). Corresponding OAB response rates were 79.4% (n = 171) and 73.9% (n = 760). Mean decreases in UUI episodes were 3.0 with iTNM and 3.5 with SNM. Weighted device-related adverse-event rates were 9.6% (n = 284) and 12.7% (n = 434), respectively. These comparable outcomes are notable because the iTNM studies did not use the preimplantation stimulation trial applied in most SNM studies.

For clinical interpretation, the evidence remains indirect. Weighted follow-up was 13.0 months for iTNM versus 39.2 months for SNM, restricting comparison of later revisions and explantation. The authors also identify variation in populations and outcome definitions, unavailable patient-level data, and moderate potential bias in 11 studies. They call for randomized comparative studies and longer iTNM follow-up.

document_sections.heading: ABSTRACT
document_sections.content: Implantable tibial neuromodulation (iTNM) has recently become commercially available in the US as another neurostimulation approach for overactive bladder (OAB). Because direct comparative studies were unavailable, this meta-analysis aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of iTNM and sacral neuromodulation (SNM) indirectly. The search covered OAB and neuromodulation. Primary efficacy measures were ≥ 50% reductions in urgency urinary incontinence (UUI) episodes, urinary frequency, and/or OAB symptoms; the primary safety measure included device-related adverse events (AEs). The 20 eligible studies included 1416 SNM-treated patients and 350 iTNM-treated patients. No direct comparative or placebo-controlled studies of SNM and iTNM were found, so the analysis used single-arm outcomes. Weighted UUI responder rates were 71.8% for SNM and 71.3% for iTNM; weighted OAB responder rates were 73.9% and 79.4%, respectively. Device-related AE rates were also similar. The authors concluded that both approaches had similar efficacy and safety for OAB and UUI, including symptom responses, fewer UUI episodes, significant quality-of-life (QoL) improvements, and low procedure- and device-related AE rates. Comparable efficacy occurred even though the iTNM studies did not use a preliminary neuromodulation trial, unlike the SNM studies.

document_sections.heading: Key Summary Points Why carry out this study?
document_sections.content: iTNM systems became available in the US within the past two years and offer a less invasive implantable option for OAB, a condition with substantial effects on QoL. The analysis indirectly compared iTNM with SNM, the most commonly used implantable neuromodulation approach for OAB, to inform decisions by clinicians and patients.

document_sections.heading: What was learned from this study?
document_sections.content: The analysis indicated that iTNM appears to offer efficacy and safety similar to SNM and may provide another treatment choice for patients with OAB. Randomized comparative studies remain important to clarify similarities and differences between the approaches.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: OAB affects millions worldwide and is more prevalent among older adults; approximately one in six adults in the US and Europe are estimated to have it. Patients may experience substantial distress and report more anxiety and depressive symptoms than healthy controls, potentially reflecting embarrassment and disruption of daily life. Possible contributors to symptoms include hormonal changes associated with menstruation, pregnancy, or menopause; postpartum changes; aging; previous bladder or pelvic surgery; pelvic floor muscle disorders; and neurological conditions such as Parkinson’s, multiple sclerosis, stroke, and spinal cord injuries. In most patients, no specific cause can be identified, and the condition is termed idiopathic. OAB symptoms can comprise urgency, frequency, nocturia, and UUI. Its prevalence and effects on QoL sustain the need for effective, safe treatments. Earlier American Urological Association (AUA) and Society of Urodynamics, Female Pelvic Medicine, and Urogenital Reconstruction (SUFU) guidelines organized OAB treatments into first-, second-, and third-line options. Their 2024 update removed the traditional step-therapy approach, emphasized shared decision-making, and arranged treatments by perceived invasiveness. It no longer requires failure of every conservative and pharmacological treatment before a minimally invasive procedure can be initiated.

document_sections.heading: Overview of Current Treatment Options for OAB
document_sections.content: Non-invasive approaches historically designated first-line include dietary and behavioral changes, bladder retraining, pelvic floor muscle physiotherapy, and transcutaneous or transvaginal pelvic floor electrical stimulation. The cited guidance and studies describe combined approaches as most successful. In selected patients, these options moderately reduce OAB and UUI symptoms, but their results have been inconsistent and limited compared with pharmacotherapy; combining them with OAB medication is therefore often recommended. Pharmacotherapy, until recently considered second-line, commonly uses anticholinergic agents or beta-adrenergic agonists. Although effective for some patients, anticholinergics can cause dry mouth, dry eyes, headache, and constipation; more than 50% of patients stop OAB medication during their first treatment year. Concern about a potential association between prolonged anticholinergic use and dementia risk has also discouraged continued use. Current AUA/SUFU guidelines identify percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS), iTNM, SNM, and botulinum toxin injection (“Botox”; BTX) as minimally invasive procedures with high success, durable efficacy, and excellent patient satisfaction. These formerly third-line options have shown the greatest success in reducing OAB/UUI symptoms, particularly when conservative treatment fails, and results in older patients are promising. Acupuncture is also minimally invasive, but less efficacy evidence is available. Bladder BTX reduces OAB and UUI symptoms and has shown efficacy similar to SNM. Because its effect diminishes as BTX is metabolized, injections must be repeated every 3–6 months, creating inconvenience and cumulative cost. AUA/SUFU guidelines recommend checking post-void residual after BTX to verify adequate emptying; patients with substantial voiding difficulty may need temporary catheterization. Other possible complications include peri-procedural urinary tract infection (UTI) and hematuria. SNM electrically stimulates the S3 sacral nerve root. It was FDA-approved in 1997 and has established efficacy for OAB and UUI. The traditional 2-stage procedure involves 2 separate procedures: a stimulation trial, typically lasting 1–3 weeks, identifies responders before permanent implantable pulse generator (IPG) placement. That trial can use an office peripheral nerve evaluation (PNE) or initial surgical placement of a permanent tined lead. Despite its efficacy, SNM may entail reprogramming and surgery for lead revision or battery replacement; an SNM trial can also be considered after BTX failure. PTNS accesses a peripheral nerve to modulate the pelvic plexus. Cleared for US commercial use in 2000, it is delivered in an office using a thin needle resembling an acupuncture needle. Cited studies established efficacy for mild-to-moderate OAB, including against sham treatment, and described clinically comparable efficacy to tolterodine tartrate (Detrol LA). Drawbacks include frequent office visits to obtain and maintain a response and variation in needle-placement skill. Recent evidence of benefit from transcutaneous tibial nerve stimulation in dry-OAB further supports the tibial nerve as an OAB treatment target. Like SNM, iTNM provides a permanent implant, placed subcutaneously or beneath the fascia at the ankle; stimulation can occur at home rather than through frequent office visits. iTNM became commercially available in the US in 2022, following promising pivotal-study results for UUI. For patients who are refractory to, or have contraindications to, all first-, second-, and third-line treatments, AUA/SUFU guidelines acknowledge more aggressive options: bladder augmentation cystoplasty, urinary diversion, and chronic indwelling catheters.

document_sections.heading: Current Analysis
document_sections.content: Neuromodulation was first approved in the US for OAB nearly 30 years ago. Subsequent innovations have aimed to improve efficacy and safety. Two iTNM systems, Revi (BlueWind) and eCoin (Valencia), have recently become commercially available. Although these options are less invasive than available SNM procedures, their relative efficacy and safety remain important questions, and randomized direct comparisons had not yet been completed. This systematic review and meta-analysis sought to quantify similarities and differences in outcomes for patients with OAB symptoms through an indirect comparison of iTNM and SNM studies.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: The authors conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and prospectively registered it as PROSPERO ID CRD42024549598. Objectives, search methods, eligibility rules, outcomes, quality assessment, and statistical methods were specified beforehand. The article analyzed previously conducted studies and involved no new human or animal study performed by its authors.

document_sections.heading: Literature‑Search Strategy
document_sections.content: A systematic search in May 2024 initially imposed no language, regional, or publication-type restrictions. It sought randomized controlled trials (RCTs), comparative studies, and single-arm cohorts addressing efficacy and safety of iTNM or SNM for OAB and/or UUI. PubMed and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) were searched electronically. The PICOS search elements appear in Supplementary Table S2 (A and B); both databases used the same terms, adapted to their formatting requirements. Nonsystematic manual searching in Google Scholar supplemented the electronic search.

document_sections.heading: Study Selection
document_sections.content: Key eligibility requirements were permanent SNM or iTNM implantation, an adult population, publication after January 1, 2010, and a prospective or retrospective clinical study or randomized trial with ≥ 15 patients. Exclusions covered non-human research; reviews, study protocols, and health-economic studies; populations consisting only of patients with previous SNM/iTNM failure or already using previously implanted devices; populations outside OAB and/or UUI; simultaneous use of multiple minimally invasive treatments; studies lacking any primary efficacy or safety endpoint for this meta-analysis; and articles unavailable in English. After duplicate and retracted records were removed, two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, then two reviewers independently assessed potentially eligible full texts. Discussion resolved discrepancies, with a third reviewer arbitrating disagreements. Prior or current OAB treatment and traditional second-line medication use did not themselves restrict eligibility. When publications shared patients across follow-up reports, the report with the longest follow-up was chosen. The prespecified plan stated that, if high-risk-of-bias publications constituted less than 15% of selected citations, they would be listed in the bias assessment but excluded from further data extraction.

document_sections.heading: Data Extraction and Assessment of Bias
document_sections.content: Two reviewers independently extracted study design, demographics, device, patient number, mean age, gender, baseline OAB symptoms, follow-up duration, primary efficacy and safety outcomes, secondary outcomes, and QoL measures. Missing values were not imputed. When several follow-up points were reported, the longest was used. No study supplied patient-level data; extraction relied on published results and did not use automation. Discrepancies were discussed and unresolved disagreements went to a third reviewer. Primary diary-based efficacy measures, when available, were the proportions with ≥ 50% improvement in study-defined composite OAB symptoms, UUI symptoms, or urinary frequency (UF). Primary safety measures included reported device- or procedure-related adverse events and, where reported, infection, pain, lead migration, wound-healing problems, surgical revision or removal, and reasons for reintervention. Secondary efficacy measures were mean UUI-episode reduction, mean urinary-frequency change, and short-term (< 6 month) UUI effects. Patient-reported measures included the Overactive Bladder Questionnaire (OAB-q), other QoL measures, and satisfaction.

document_sections.heading: Data Synthesis and Analysis
document_sections.content: The bias assessment considered nine equally weighted areas: design, number of centers, randomization, blinding, standardized patient-reported primary efficacy measurement, attrition, follow-up duration, AE reporting, and industry funding. Lower bias was assumed for prospective, multicenter, randomized, blinded studies with standardized measures such as bladder diaries, follow-up longer than 6 months, low attrition, AE reporting, and no industry funding. Higher bias was assumed for retrospective, single-center, single-arm or unblinded studies; subjective primary measures; follow-up of 6 months or less; high attrition; reports of zero AEs; and industry funding. Attrition below 10% per year was considered lower risk: illustrative proportions retained at 1, 2, or 3 years were 90.0%, 81.0% or 72.9%, respectively. Aggregate ratings of 0–3, 4–6, and 7–9 denoted low, moderate, and high bias. For available primary efficacy and safety outcomes, the authors calculated weighted averages separately for iTNM and SNM. Because eligible designs varied, they also separated interventional studies (RCTs and prospective interventions) from observational studies (prospective observational studies and retrospective reviews). Descriptive statistics and weighted averages were calculated in Microsoft Excel; GraphPad Prism and Microsoft Excel were used for figures.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: PubMed and Cochrane CENTRAL yielded 1185 citations, and a nonsystematic Google Scholar search identified one additional article. Removal of 105 duplicates and 2 retracted articles left 1079 abstracts; 934 were excluded at abstract screening. Of 145 full texts assessed, 124 were excluded. A further study [54] was excluded after assessment because of high bias risk, leaving 20 studies in the meta-analysis. The selection flow is shown in Fig. 1. The text reports nine studies with low bias, eleven with moderate bias, and one with high bias in the assessment; the high-risk study was not included in outcome extraction. Most studies were unblinded, partly because perceived stimulation makes blinding difficult when comparing neuromodulation approaches. Two studies [55, 56] used a single-blind period of 3 months to compare standard with delayed activation before continuing unblinded treatment. Because the meta-analysis selected the latest available follow-up, all primary endpoint data came from patients who knew which treatment they received. The Fig. 2 description specifies low, moderate, and high potential bias as 0–2, 3–5, and 6 or more assessed areas, respectively; these cutoffs differ from those stated in the methods.

document_sections.heading: Patient Populations and Risk of Bias Across Studies
document_sections.content: The 20 included studies comprised three RCTs [30, 55, 57], ten prospective interventional studies [51, 52, 56, 58–64], one prospective observational study [65], and six retrospective chart reviews [66–71]. They included 1766 patients: 350 received iTNM in 4 studies and 1416 received SNM in 16 studies. For iTNM, weighted mean age was 61.2 years (n = 350), 98.0% were female (n = 350), follow-up ranged from 12 months to 3 years, and weighted follow-up was 13.0 months. For SNM, weighted mean age was 57.0 years (n = 1416), 87.5% were female (n = 1416), final follow-up ranged from 6 months to 9.7 years, and weighted follow-up was 39.2 months. Table 1 presents study designs and demographics. Available follow-up differed between newer iTNM technology, described here as FDA-approved in 2022, and established SNM, described here as FDA-approved in 1996. Baseline disease-severity measures were similar across studies. Most patients had UUI: weighted averages were 98.9% for iTNM (n = 350) and 83.3% for SNM (n = 1107). Prior oral medication use was reported for 92.6% of iTNM patients (n = 330) and 99.7% of SNM patients (n = 1175). Weighted baseline UUI episodes per day were 4.6 with iTNM (n = 350) and 5.0 with SNM (n = 1150). Few studies reported symptom duration, potentially because recall may be unreliable; all studies that did report it found a mean of 4 or more years of OAB symptoms before neurostimulation. Concurrent oral OAB medication at baseline was a possible confounder: many studies did not report it and some [52, 55, 61–65] included medicated patients. Reported baseline symptoms reflected OAB severity while such medications were being used.

document_sections.heading: Efficacy Measures: Improvements to OAB Symptoms
document_sections.content: Diary-based primary outcomes were the percentages of patients achieving ≥ 50% improvement in UUI, composite OAB symptoms, or UF. Secondary outcomes included mean UUI-episode reduction, mean urinary-frequency change, and short-term (< 6 month) UUI effects. UUI response was available from four iTNM and eight SNM studies: weighted responder rates were 71.3% (n = 350) and 71.8% (n = 950), respectively. OAB response was available from two iTNM and eight SNM studies, with weighted rates of 79.4% for iTNM and 73.9% for SNM. Table 2 presents study-level primary efficacy results; study-specific definitions are in Supplementary Table S5. Although UF response was planned as a primary outcome, none of the four iTNM studies reported it, preventing comparison with SNM; results from the six applicable SNM studies appear in Supplementary Table S6. Analyses by study type produced broadly similar findings. SNM interventional and observational results were generally alike, with differences mainly influenced by particularly favorable results in two interventional Axonics studies [58, 59]. All four iTNM studies were interventional. Weighted UUI response was 71.3% (n = 350) for interventional iTNM, 74.0% (n = 661) for interventional SNM, and 66.5% (n = 289) for observational SNM. Weighted OAB response was 79.4% (n = 171), 82.5% (n = 393), and 64.7% (n = 367), respectively. Weighted mean decreases in UUI episodes were 3.0 (n = 350) with iTNM and 3.5 (n = 1150) with SNM. Weighted urinary-frequency decreases were 2.0 (n = 304) and 5.5 (n = 1041), respectively. The authors considered this apparent difference likely related to differing baseline frequencies: 10.2 (n = 171) versus 15.1 (n = 1041) voids per day, respectively. Studies conducted in Asia reported significantly higher baseline frequencies of 21.6–29.2 voids per day [55, 56, 62, 70] and largely drove the baseline difference. At 3 and 6 months, weighted proportions with ≥ 50% fewer UUI episodes were 76.8% (n = 631) and 67.9% (n = 721) for SNM, compared with 69.0% (n = 197) and 74.4% (n = 304) for iTNM. Table 3 summarizes secondary endpoints, with additional study-specific and short-term results in Supplementary Tables S7, S8, and S9.

document_sections.heading: Positive Impacts on Quality of Life (QoL)
document_sections.content: The analysis used the aggregate health-related quality of life (HRQoL) score from OAB-q, a commonly used OAB instrument; its minimally important difference was ≥ 10 points. Weighted proportions reaching a ≥ 10-point HRQoL change were 83.2% (n = 171) for iTNM and 48.4% (n = 340) for SNM. Only two SNM studies contributed to that weighted estimate, and one [57] had substantially lower HRQoL scores. Weighted mean HRQoL score increases were 34.5 points (n = 133) with iTNM and 35.1 points (n = 427) with SNM. The proportions attaining a patient global impression of improvement (PGI-I) rating of ≥ “better” were 88.5% (n = 197) and 74.9% (n = 207), respectively. Reported treatment satisfaction, available less often, was 95% (n = 151) for iTNM and 75.5% (n = 334) for SNM. Table 3 also presents QoL and satisfaction results.

document_sections.heading: Revisions, Explants, and Lead Migrations
document_sections.content: Table 4 presents permanent explantation, surgical revision, and lead-migration rates. The authors describe weighted rates across those outcomes as 0–1.7% in iTNM studies versus 5.6–26.8% in SNM studies. The table gives weighted permanent explantation rates of 1.0% for iTNM and 13.7% for SNM, surgical revision rates of 0.0% and 26.8%, and migration rates of 1.7% and 5.6%, respectively. The iTNM migration rate of 1.7% occurred despite ankle movement and might reflect device construction. eCoin occupies an implanted tissue pocket and has a larger surface area than a thin lead, potentially limiting displacement. Revi has 4 holes for sutures that can secure it to fascia; its flat subcutaneous position may also reduce migration associated with patient manipulation. Common reasons for surgical revision were battery depletion requiring exchange, lead migration, electrode failure, diminished effectiveness, and AEs such as infection.

document_sections.heading: Safety Measures
document_sections.content: Revision risk can accumulate over a device’s implanted lifetime, whereas most device- or procedure-related AEs generally arise during the first several months after implantation. Weighted device-related serious AE rates were 0.3% (n = 350) for iTNM and 3.3% (n = 892) for SNM; device-related AE rates were 9.6% (n = 284) and 12.7% (n = 434); procedure-related AE rates were 10.6% (n = 151) and 11.6% (n = 129), respectively. The authors characterized both approaches as having favorable safety profiles and similar weighted infection, pain, and wound-healing rates, presented in Table 5. Risks may vary among devices within each category: published device-related AE rates were 4.0% for Revi and 16.0% for eCoin.

document_sections.heading: DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: Neuromodulation has been accepted for lower urinary tract dysfunction unresponsive to behavioral and/or drug treatment for more than 25 years. Since the late 1990s, SNM has had established efficacy and a favorable safety profile for OAB; the sacral nerves contain many motor and sensory elements and are important stimulation targets. Experience with effective, safe PTNS has supported exploration of other peripheral targets for pelvic dysfunction, including urinary incontinence, despite the repeated treatments and patient and healthcare burdens associated with percutaneous stimulation. Implantable tibial technologies developed from that experience. As minimally invasive OAB treatment becomes more common, this meta-analysis supports similar efficacy and safety for iTNM and SNM despite differences in stimulation site, implantation, and treatment schedule. Patient satisfaction and PGI-I showed a trend favoring iTNM. Most permanent SNM implants involve sedation or general anesthesia, whereas most iTNM procedures use local anesthesia; sedation for iTNM can be chosen but is not required. Sacral lead implantation needs fluoroscopy, while iTNM does not, reducing radiation exposure to clinicians and patients. Available SNM devices implant both a lead and a neurostimulator; eCoin and Revi each use a single-piece implant. Together these features generally make iTNM implantation less invasive, although individual patient and clinician preferences remain relevant and both procedures had favorable safety findings. The posterior tibial and sacral nerves arise at similar spinal cord levels and can stimulate the same neural network, offering a plausible explanation for comparable efficacy. Both approaches target the sacral nerve plexus, but their initial stimulation and implant locations differ: iTNM is placed at the inner ankle above the medial malleolus, while SNM places a lead along the S(sacral)3 nerve root in the lower back and generally places the IPG, including its battery, beneath the skin of the upper buttock. Anesthesia, fluoroscopy, procedure time, implanted hardware, and patient interaction also vary by device. Adjustable polarity, current delivery, frequency, and pulse width matter to neuromodulation efficacy and durability. Altering settings over time has been used to sustain responses and help patients whose initial settings did not achieve treatment goals; the capacity for patients or clinicians to adjust settings differs among devices. A cited patient-preference survey [75] suggested that iTNM might increase interest in minimally invasive OAB treatment. Comparable efficacy is notable because iTNM studies did not use an initial stimulation trial to select responders. SNM ordinarily uses a PNE wire or a surgically placed tined lead for that trial, excluding nonresponders from permanent implantation and subsequent study follow-up. Of 16 included SNM studies, 14 used a PNE or staged trial, while only 2 Axonics studies [58, 59] did not. Across trials, weighted failure was 27%; the meta-analysis included only permanently implanted SNM patients. The authors describe the ARTISAN Axonics study [59], which did not require a trial, as having the most favorable SNM efficacy results. Longer iTNM follow-up is needed to determine whether comparable efficacy persists without preimplantation selection. Included SNM studies used continuous stimulation, while all four iTNM studies used varying cyclic schedules. Possible reduction in nerve habituation and hypothesized later efficacy loss with cyclic treatment remain under investigation, including in SNM; nevertheless, efficacy appeared similar despite less frequent iTNM stimulation. Permanently implanted devices can require surgery when problems occur. Fixed batteries require replacement after depletion, an important contributor to the 26.8% all-cause surgical reintervention rate in the included SNM studies. The authors anticipate that longer-lived implanted batteries, rechargeable systems, or external batteries may reduce future battery-exchange surgery; recently introduced longer-life SNM options may therefore yield lower reintervention rates with longer follow-up. Rechargeable and external batteries require patient participation, which may be viewed favorably or unfavorably. Revi has a wearable external battery and is recommended for use at least once a day for 30 min. Some patients may prefer implanted, non-rechargeable ‘set and forget’ options, including InterStim, Axonics, and eCoin; others may value control of treatment delivery. In the cited ARTISAN-SNM study [59], rechargeable SNM required interaction every 1–2 weeks and was accompanied by favorable follow-up and outcomes. In the cited OASIS study [52], Revi required interaction at least twice daily, and 94% of patients said at 12 months that they were willing to continue. Further evidence is needed to understand how device interaction affects patient selection. Delivering neuromodulation on demand when needed remains a future challenge. Guideline changes may allow implantation earlier in the course of pelvic floor conditions, potentially avoiding prolonged primary and secondary treatments associated with substantial dissatisfaction. The authors view the availability of both iTNM and SNM as progress for OAB care. In view of concerns about a potential anticholinergic–dementia association, neuromodulation offers an effective nonpharmacological alternative consistent with AUA/SUFU support for earlier consideration of minimally invasive treatment.

document_sections.heading: Limitations
document_sections.content: Despite the number of included studies and patients, 11 studies had moderate potential bias, often because stimulation sensation complicates randomization and blinding and because several studies were retrospective or single-center. Variation in populations, geography, methods, efficacy definitions, and device-development stage—from pilot through pivotal to postmarketing research—may limit generalizability. Patient-level data were unavailable, and endpoint results were not available from every study even when an endpoint had been collected. Weighted follow-up differed between iTNM and SNM studies: 13.0 versus 39.2 months, respectively. The authors relate this to SNM’s nearly 30 years of US commercial availability since 1996, compared with iTNM’s FDA approval less than 2 years earlier, in December 2022. They note that most device- and procedure-related AEs arise in the first several months for both approaches, but later revision and explantation rates still need comparison. Implanted batteries in either approach will eventually require surgical replacement. Initial implantation and revision impose costs on patients and healthcare systems, yet published iTNM-versus-SNM cost comparisons were unavailable. Urinary-frequency comparisons were also difficult: studies from North America, Europe, and the Middle East reported baseline frequencies of 10–14.9, while Asian SNM studies reported 21.6–29.2. The reason is uncertain; the Asian studies may represent patients with more severe OAB. The effect of iTNM on urinary frequency warrants further study. No identified study directly compared iTNM with SNM. Future RCTs are needed to clarify comparative efficacy, safety, and appropriate patient selection.

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
document_sections.content: Across 20 clinical studies involving 1766 patients with OAB, iTNM and SNM produced similar clinical benefit, including comparable proportions with ≥ 50% reductions in UUI episodes and OAB symptoms, reductions in UUI-episode counts, and improvements in QoL. Comparable efficacy was observed despite the absence of a neuromodulation trial phase in the iTNM studies, in contrast to the SNM studies. Current results suggest that iTNM may have fewer surgical reinterventions, but longer follow-up is required to determine whether that pattern persists. Procedure- and device-related AE rates were low with both approaches.
